data.title: AlgoBrain BCI
data.summary: A custom bio-amplifier and embedded signal-processing prototype for device control.

projects.body:
## Problem

AlgoBrain began with a simple but demanding goal: turn a weak biological signal into a reliable physical action. The prototype explored using forehead electrodes to control a light or relay, but it also exposed the hard part of a brain-computer interface: signals from people are small, noisy, inconsistent across users, and easy to confuse with motion, muscle activity, and electrical interference.

This was a research prototype, not a clinical device and not a claim of dependable thought control. Its value was the full engineering chain: an analog front end, embedded acquisition, digital signal processing, visualization, and a hardware output that made the quality of the decision visible.

## What I built

I designed a custom TL074 bio-amplifier and PCB, built the enclosure and prototype hardware, and developed Arduino firmware for acquisition and control. The project files include circuit and PCB work, SPICE exploration, breadboard and recorded tests, 3D-print files, Arduino sketches, a Processing visual client, and a later Python visualizer for recording and analysis.

The analog path uses a four-stage operational-amplifier arrangement: differential acquisition, high-pass filtering, gain, and low-pass filtering. The electrode setup in the project notes uses a forehead channel with ear-mounted references. Its job is to move a microvolt-scale biological signal into the Arduino's ADC range while rejecting as much common noise and drift as practical.

The project was deliberately end to end. It did not stop at displaying a waveform: the sender can transmit processed samples over serial, and a separate receiver sketch can interpret an IR command and drive a relay with red/green status indicators.

## How it works

### Analog signal before software

Biological signals are unforgiving of poor front-end design. The amplifier has to preserve a useful signal while the electrodes, mains interference, body movement, and the ADC reference all introduce unwanted variation. The TL074 circuit and its filter stages were the first attempt to create a signal that firmware could work with at all.

That also explains why the project is more accurately described as EEG/EMG experimentation. The hardware and code were used to investigate a forehead-based signal path, but a visible response can come from muscle activity or motion as well as any intended EEG pattern. Treating those sources as separable is a key requirement for a stronger second version.

### Sampling, filtering, and envelope detection

The active data-sender sketch targets 500 samples per second from analog pin A0 and emits raw value, filtered value, and a cycle counter at 115200 baud. The firmware implements four cascaded second-order filter sections using persistent state variables, then produces a serial stream that can be inspected outside the microcontroller.

The controller sketch follows the same signal path but adds a 128-sample circular-buffer envelope. It rectifies the filtered signal, averages the recent history, applies a sensitivity factor, and compares the result with a threshold to drive an LED. At the intended 500 Hz cadence, a 128-sample window represents roughly 256 ms of history: enough to smooth a transient, but still short enough to make control feel responsive.

There is an important archival detail: the data-sender uses a `1,000,000 / SAMPLE_RATE` microsecond timer interval, while the older controller sketch uses `10,000,000 / SAMPLE_RATE`. The latter schedules ten times more slowly than its 500 Hz label suggests. The files document the prototype honestly: the timing needs to be verified on the exact sketch and hardware being demonstrated.

### From signal to an external action

The serial path made the prototype observable. The later Python visualizer keeps five seconds of raw and filtered data, plots a 0–50 Hz spectrum, reports basic signal statistics, and supports recording sessions for future analysis. This is the bridge between an embedded experiment and a dataset: it makes it possible to compare a user action with the signal that preceded it instead of tuning a threshold by feel alone.

The output side was kept separate. An IR receiver sketch listens for a received command, changes relay state, illuminates a red or green status indicator, and blocks repeated triggers for five seconds. This split makes the design easier to debug: signal acquisition, visual feedback, and the physical output can each be tested independently.

## Result

AlgoBrain placed fourth among more than 150 teams at the national innovation competition in Rades. More importantly, it produced a working record of the decisions behind a bio-signal prototype: analog amplification, custom PCB work, fixed-rate embedded acquisition, digital filtering, envelope-based control, serial visualization, and a relay output.

The prototype also revealed its limits clearly. A fixed threshold can work for a controlled demonstration but cannot account for electrode placement, user differences, fatigue, movement, or an unstable baseline. That evidence is valuable because it turns AlgoBrain v2 into a specific engineering problem rather than an abstract AI idea.

## What I would improve

AlgoBrain v2 should start with synchronized data collection: record the raw signal, filtered signal, event label, user, electrode placement, and session conditions together. Calibration should establish a per-user baseline before any control threshold is chosen. Artifact checks should explicitly flag blinks, movement, and obvious EMG contamination instead of treating every high envelope as intent.

On the hardware side, I would validate the analog front end with known inputs, document ADC scaling and the actual sampling rate, and add a clear safety boundary between the sensing electronics and any power output. On the software side, I would compare the current envelope baseline with simple spectral features and a small personalized classifier only after the recorded data shows a repeatable signal. The goal is not to make a bigger claim; it is to make each decision in the control chain measurable.

data.title: AquaFlow
data.summary: Fish-water monitoring with custom AC-based TDS sensing, ESP32 controls and a mobile dashboard.

projects.body:
## Problem
A fish-water system is only useful when its physical flow, measurements and operating controls are legible in the same place. AquaFlow explored that connection with a small water-tank test bench: make the equipment observable, give an operator clear status signals, and provide a practical control surface rather than treating the hardware as a black box.

The challenge was not only to assemble the plumbing and electronics. The prototype had to make a changing fish-water setup understandable: what the water level and quality readings are saying, which equipment is available to control, and when the system needs attention.

That required the same sensing foundation developed for Plantini, but applied to a different operating context. A TDS reading has to be treated as a measurement with uncertainty, not as an unquestioned dashboard number: it needs a calibration context and a controller that can tell the difference between a usable reading and one that is stale, unsettled or implausible.

## What I built
AquaFlow brings together three tangible pieces of the prototype:

- A **water-tank test bench** with the tank, tubing and connected equipment used to exercise the physical setup.
- A **controller enclosure** containing the control electronics and a multi-channel relay board for connecting equipment.
- A **mobile control dashboard** that presents the system state and the operating controls in one interface.
- A **proprietary AC-based TDS sensing path** and ESP32 control layer, adapted from the in-house technology developed for Plantini.

The TDS sensor, its AC excitation, analog conditioning, calibration routine and production firmware are proprietary. As with Plantini, the aim is to keep the sensing technology understandable and manufacturable in-house while protecting the implementation details that make it work.

The gallery separates the real prototype from the illustrative water-system diagram. The diagram communicates the intended flow path; the bench, wiring, enclosure and demonstration document the hardware that was actually assembled.

## How it works
### From the tank to a readable state

The mobile dashboard is organized around the conditions that matter to a fish-water operator: temperature, TDS and water level. In the captured interface, an urgent low-water warning and a high-TDS warning are surfaced before the lower-level controls, so attention is drawn to the condition before an action is taken.

The proprietary sensor measures a property of the water that AquaFlow uses as a TDS proxy. The AC approach avoids a persistent DC bias at the interface with the water. An ESP32 receives the conditioned sensor output, applies the private calibration and decision logic, and exposes a usable state to the rest of the system.

### From a control screen to hardware

The same dashboard groups equipment controls into clear cards, including compressor and filter/pump controls. The controller enclosure shows the corresponding physical side of that design: an ESP32-based control board, power hardware and relay wiring are housed together so the prototype can connect interface-level choices to external equipment.

The private firmware is responsible for more than passing a number to the screen. A reliable control layer needs to consider whether the reading is fresh, whether the water has settled after an equipment change, and whether a deviation is meaningful enough to surface as an alert. Those decisions remain private; the public design is the path from fish water, through a calibrated sensing layer, to a readable operating state.

### A prototype, not a product claim

The concept diagram is an illustrative system view, while the tank, controller and video are the evidence of the working prototype. Together they show the direction of the system without overstating long-term reliability, sensor accuracy or production readiness.

## Result
The result is a documented end-to-end prototype: a physical fish-water setup, a controller enclosure, proprietary in-house sensing technology, a mobile monitoring and control surface, and a demonstration of the assembled system. It gives the project a concrete bridge between the water system, the electronics and the person operating it.

Most importantly, the project evidence now makes the process visible. Rather than presenting only a diagram or only an app screen, AquaFlow shows the proprietary sensing context, the control experience and the hardware it is connected to.

## What I would improve
The next iteration should turn the prototype record into a measurable operating story:

- Run long-duration sensing tests with raw and calibrated readings, reference checks and maintenance events to understand drift and repeatability in fish water.
- Document the safe operating ranges and calibration approach behind the temperature, TDS and water-level states.
- Record time-series telemetry so alerts can be reviewed against real tank behaviour rather than a single screen state.
- Define safe actuator defaults, manual overrides and interlocks for pump, filter and compressor control.
- Add a repeatable test plan that covers low-water, high-TDS and connectivity-loss scenarios.

Those additions would make it possible to evaluate the system's behaviour as an engineered product, not only as an assembled prototype.

data.title: Cleenolve
data.summary: A thermal-inspection interface for locating possible solar-panel hotspots.

projects.body:
## Problem
Solar installations are large, repetitive, and difficult to inspect panel by panel. A thermal camera can turn temperature differences into a visible pattern, but that is only the start of the job. Reflections, hot surroundings, junctions, and image texture can all create bright regions that look important at first glance.

The useful outcome is not simply a colourful thermal frame. It is a short, reviewable list of locations that may need a technician to inspect.

## What I built
Cleenolve brings that review process into a focused thermal hotspot detector. The recorded interface accepts a video file or a live stream, displays the thermal image, draws candidate boxes, and reports the number of current candidates.

The controls expose the decisions that change a detector's behaviour: sensitivity, the largest permitted box as a percentage of the frame, minimum spot size, texture filtering, and a cluster filter. That makes the tool an inspection aid with visible tuning controls rather than a black box that silently decides what is faulty.

The project also includes a solar-cleaning robot render. It is a concept for the operational side of the wider idea, not evidence of a tested autonomous robot.

## How it works
### Start from thermal contrast, then constrain the result
The interface starts by identifying bright thermal regions relative to the rest of the frame. Raising sensitivity restricts the candidates to hotter regions; lowering it can reveal weaker temperature differences but also introduces more noise. A field workflow needs both settings because a threshold that works at one time of day or with one camera palette may fail elsewhere.

### Reject shapes that do not fit the inspection task
A fault candidate should have a plausible size in the image. The maximum-box control can discard very large warm areas, such as a whole roof zone, while the minimum-spot control removes tiny isolated pixels. These are practical safeguards: without them, a detector can spend its time reporting things that are either too broad to localise or too small to investigate.

### Use texture and density as evidence, not as a verdict
Thermal images contain texture from module boundaries, ground, reflections, and compression. The texture filter offers a way to suppress candidates that do not have the local variation expected by the chosen settings. The cluster filter addresses another failure mode: many overlapping boxes can turn one confusing region into a long list of alerts. Grouping or suppressing dense clusters makes the overlay easier to read.

These controls are only a first pass. A box is a candidate for inspection, not a confirmed electrical fault. Confirmation needs context such as panel layout, irradiance, camera calibration, repeat observations, and where appropriate an electrical measurement.

## Result
The supplied evidence shows a working inspection interface with video and stream controls, adjustable filters, and hotspot overlays on a solar-array thermal frame. It demonstrates the review workflow and the kinds of false positives the controls are intended to manage.

It does not establish detection accuracy, camera calibration, fault-classification performance, or robot field performance. Those require labelled thermal data and on-site validation.

## What I would improve
I would add a frame-by-frame review queue that keeps the source timestamp, panel-row position, detector settings, and an operator decision for every alert. Requiring a candidate to persist across adjacent frames would reduce one-frame noise. A calibration and validation plan should compare the alerts with confirmed field findings, then report precision and missed defects separately for different weather conditions.

For the robot concept, the next concrete milestone is a safe manual or supervised platform test: traction, panel-safe contact forces, water use, obstacle handling, and an emergency-stop path all need evidence before autonomy becomes a meaningful claim.

data.title: Cyclops
data.summary: A staged research engine turning a clarified question into organized web and paper evidence.

projects.body:
## Problem
Deep research fails in several ways before writing begins. The question may be too vague, results may repeat the same source, a paper may be unavailable, or a PDF may hide important information inside figures and tables.

Cyclops treats research as a sequence of evidence-processing tasks. Its goal is to turn an initial question into a clearer brief, collect relevant web and academic material, and produce organized reports that retain connections to their sources.

## What I built
I built a Python workflow with separate stages for interviewing the user, generating queries, collecting sources, removing duplicates, downloading documents, extracting information, and writing reports. The implementation is private; this article focuses on its behavior and architecture.

The supplied cover is a concept overview. The reviewed implementation is a staged research pipeline, so the illustrated interface and feature labels should not be treated as proof that every depicted screen is implemented.

## How it works
### Start with a research brief
The opening stage collects research intent and source preferences. Query generation expands the brief into searches appropriate to the topic. Later analysis uses that intent and its relevance criteria when deciding which information is useful.

Finding a document and finding an answer are different tasks. A broadly related paper may appear in search results without supporting the specific question being investigated.

### Process papers and web pages differently
The academic path discovers paper links, removes repeated results, resolves document locations, and downloads PDFs. An additional search path looks for alternative document sources when the first route is insufficient. Another deduplication pass limits repeated work across sources.

PDF analysis goes beyond treating a document as one plain text block. The implementation examines page complexity and includes paths for text extraction, tables, OCR, and rendered page images. Complex pages can be processed differently from ordinary text pages, preserving information a text-only pass may overlook.

The web path collects URLs, deduplicates them, and retrieves content through browser workers. Saved pages are analyzed in batches before their results are assembled into a web report. Keeping the paths separate lets the extraction method match the material.

### Make intermediate work visible
Query lists, filtered URLs, extracted content, and analysis outputs are saved between stages. These artifacts help locate where a weak result began: discovery, download, extraction, relevance filtering, or synthesis.

The sequence runner executes stages in order and stops when a stage fails or a required script is missing. This prevents downstream work after an explicit process failure. It is still a simple runner, rather than a durable workflow service with automatic resumption and versioned checkpoints.

### Preserve a route back to evidence
Paper analysis records relevance information and produces structured summaries. The academic report combines summaries with references to retained local PDFs, while the web report follows its own collected material. Document links give the reader a route back to evidence, although links alone do not prove that each sentence is supported.

The reviewed folder contains academic and web report stages. A combined final PDF and video-research path appear in planning notes, so they are not presented here as completed outputs of this runner.

## Result
Cyclops connects question clarification, source collection, document processing, and report generation in one inspectable workflow. Its useful design idea is separating research into stages with visible inputs and outputs: a report can be improved by fixing the evidence pipeline that produced it.

The local implementation includes generated reports and intermediate analysis artifacts. No research-quality score or execution benchmark is claimed here, and private source code is not distributed with the portfolio.

## What I would improve
I would add a run manifest recording input hashes, completed stages, output locations, and failures. That would allow a failed extraction to resume without repeating successful downloads and prevent stale artifacts from entering a new report.

Citation validation should connect important statements to specific pages or passages, with uncertain findings visibly marked. URL normalization also needs care: removing all query parameters can merge genuinely different documents. A stronger pipeline would retain original URLs, use source-aware canonicalization, and compare downloaded content hashes before deciding two sources are identical.

data.title: EasyShield
data.summary: A complete face anti-spoofing pipeline, from dataset preparation to live testing.

projects.body:
## Problem

Face recognition answers who a person resembles; it does not, by itself, answer whether a camera is seeing a present person. A printed portrait or replayed screen can be accepted as an identity match unless a separate liveness step stops it first.

EasyShield began as that protective step for [NiotoShield](/projects/niotoshield). I turned the anti-spoofing work into a standalone, open-source model and tool suite for distinguishing a live face from common presentation attacks before identity recognition proceeds.

## What I built

I built EasyShield around a YOLOv12-nano classifier and the surrounding workflow needed to train and inspect it: face extraction, data augmentation, image filtering, dataset preparation, model training, and live GUI testing. The release includes trained weights, example data, Windows and Linux testing paths, and the scripts that connect those stages.

The goal was not only to train one model. It was to make the dataset and iteration process repeatable: move from source photos or video to aligned face crops, curate the samples, make a YOLO-ready split, train a run, then inspect real-time predictions with their confidence scores.

## How it works

### A liveness gate before identity matching

EasyShield treats liveness as an independent decision. A camera frame is first reduced to a face region, then the classifier labels that crop as **Real** or **Fake**. In the NiotoShield flow, a fake result stops the request before the face-recognition component compares identity embeddings. A real result can continue to the identity stage.

This separation keeps the question being answered clear. The anti-spoofing model is responsible for detecting presentation attacks; an identity recognizer is responsible for matching an enrolled person. Combining those claims into one score would make failures harder to diagnose.

### Building the dataset deliberately

The preparation tools use MTCNN to extract faces from images and video, adding a margin around the detected face and resizing crops to 640 × 640. A filtering step helps remove low-quality or badly aligned samples before they become training data. The augmentation tool then varies rotation, blur, brightness, contrast, and horizontal orientation to broaden the visual conditions represented in the dataset.

The dataset-preparation script organizes the curated images into YOLO train, validation, and test partitions and generates the dataset configuration used by the trainer. That workflow matters because liveness performance is shaped as much by the coverage and labelling of real and fake examples as by the model architecture.

### Training, testing, and reviewing predictions

The training tool produces the model weights and run metrics from a prepared dataset. The testing application loads a trained model and accepts a live camera feed or file input, displaying a Real/Fake label with a confidence score. This closes the loop between offline training results and the conditions a user sees through a camera.

The repository also documents a CUDA 11.8 and cuDNN 8.9.6 environment with a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build for GPU-backed experiments. The same project includes Linux-oriented setup notes for edge devices, where available acceleration and camera hardware determine the actual runtime behavior.

## Result

The published evaluation reports 92.30% accuracy, 88.32% precision, 97.50% recall, a 98.61% AUC, and a 6.25% equal error rate on an 8,000-image test dataset. Average inference time in that evaluation was 75.47 ms. Those are project benchmark results, not a universal deployment guarantee: camera quality, attack media, lighting, compute hardware, and the population represented in the data can all change the outcome.

EasyShield grew out of [NiotoShield](/projects/niotoshield), the complete university hardware and software project. Its open-source tools are available in the [EasyShield v2.5 repository](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5).

## What I would improve

The next evaluation should publish the exact hardware configuration, dataset splits, attack-media definitions, and per-condition metrics. I would test on cameras, screens, printers, lighting conditions, and subjects that were held out from training, then report false-accept and false-reject behavior by condition.

For a deployed access system, I would also add explicit handling for uncertain predictions and camera-quality failures. A liveness score near the decision boundary should request another capture or deny access safely; it should not silently be treated as a reliable identity decision.

data.title: EazyCode
data.summary: A training platform connecting course discovery, enrollment, and learner schedules.

projects.body: ## Problem Publishing a course catalogue is only the beginning of running a training platform. The harder work starts when a learner enrolls in several courses, an administrator changes their access, or two live sessions compete for the same person's time. EazyCode connects these workflows for a technology training platform in Tunisia. Its public catalogue covers AI, cloud computing, web development, cybersecurity, and certification-oriented training. The engineering challenge is keeping the catalogue, enrollment records, and learning spaces consistent as the programme changes. ## What I built The application combines a React and Vite frontend, React Router navigation, Firestore-backed course and enrollment data, and separate administration, learner, and trainer experiences. Course detail and account pages load through lazy imports, with a shared loading fallback rather than loading every dashboard with the landing page. Beyond the public site, the implementation includes configurable enrollment questions, coupon pricing, participant management, course scheduling, and enrollment email integration. The repository is private; this case study describes the architecture without distributing its source. ## How it works ### Treat enrollment as a relationship One of the most useful design decisions is matching enrollment records by course ID first, while retaining title matching for older records. A stable identifier survives a course rename; the compatibility path lets older data remain usable during migration. Account updates reconcile the learner's selected courses against existing enrollment rows. The process keeps and updates a matching row, creates a row for a newly selected course, and removes rows no longer represented in the selection. It also normalizes email addresses before matching them. This is more deliberate than appending another enrollment whenever an administrator saves an account. The important lesson is that reconciliation is a desired-state operation: the selected course set describes what should exist. The current implementation performs multiple Firestore operations, so the algorithm itself does not guarantee an atomic update. ### Make flexible forms predictable Enrollment questions are represented as field definitions with stable IDs, types, and required flags. The validator handles required checkboxes separately from text-like values, so a required consent-style answer cannot pass merely because a field exists. The same definitions feed a structured WhatsApp handoff message, including the course, price information, and additional responses. Pricing distinguishes percentage discounts from fixed reductions and clamps the final price at zero. These small boundaries matter: form configuration and promotion rules should remain understandable to administrators without becoming scattered UI conditions. ### Check the learner's whole schedule Scheduling checks combine account course assignments with enrollment-derived course IDs. This catches a learner whose relationship to a course exists in either representation. Session intervals include a default 15-minute gap, and conflict checks can exclude the session currently being edited. For example, a two-hour session beginning at 10:00 conflicts with another beginning at 12:10 because the transition window is still active. The overlap comparison uses strict inequalities, so an exact 15-minute boundary is allowed. Locally entered date-time values are converted to ISO timestamps before storage; consistent time-zone handling remains an important design consideration. ### Keep email transport separate The Cloudflare request handler delegates enrollment email work to a shared server module and translates failures into HTTP responses. Separating the handler from message construction makes it easier to keep deployment adapters thin and evolve the email workflow without duplicating the whole application. ## Result [EazyCode is available online](https://eazycodeacademy.com). The implementation goes beyond course presentation: it links enrollment configuration, account-course reconciliation, scheduling, and communication in one platform. The useful engineering takeaway is that education software is largely a consistency problem. A polished catalogue helps someone choose a course; stable relationships and predictable updates help the team deliver it. No enrollment, conversion, or email-delivery metrics are claimed here. ## What I would improve I would make enrollment reconciliation transactional or move it behind an authoritative server operation, then test retries and simultaneous account edits. Scheduling should use an explicit academy time zone and test daylight-saving transitions for international learners. Email delivery would benefit from idempotency keys and recorded delivery state so a retry cannot silently send duplicate messages. For a growing catalogue, I would also replace collection-wide matching with indexed queries and introduce a clear migration path that eventually retires title-based enrollment matching.

data.title: Faza3D
data.summary: A 3D-printing storefront that separates ready-to-order products from custom fabrication requests.

projects.body:
## Problem
A small 3D-printing service has two very different order types. Ready-made products should be simple to browse and order. Custom jobs need enough information to decide whether a model can be made, how much material it needs, how long it may take, and what the customer actually wants.

Treating both paths as one generic contact form hides the manufacturing decisions from the customer and creates unnecessary back-and-forth for the maker.

## What I built
Faza3D is a React storefront with a catalogue, a custom-print route, a protected admin route, and theme preferences stored in the browser. The catalogue presents a fixed set of product cards with a material weight, price, product description, and an order link to Messenger.

The custom-print screen accepts either a model file or a model link, collects colour, infill, contact details, and notes, then shows an immediate planning estimate. It accepts common fabrication inputs including STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, and STP. The supplied gallery also documents the physical side of the service: finished prints and multiple printer setups.

## How it works
### Keep catalogue checkout lightweight
The catalogue is deliberately direct. Product information is defined in the frontend, and each card sends the buyer to the same Messenger ordering channel. That can be a reasonable early operating model: customers ask questions in a familiar channel and the maker can confirm stock, colour, and delivery before accepting an order.

It also exposes the limit of the current approach. Stock, orders, payments, and fulfilment status are not modelled as a transactional storefront, so Messenger is the handoff point rather than an integrated checkout.

### Ask for fabrication inputs before estimating
Custom printing needs more than a picture. The order form asks where the model comes from, the requested colour, infill, and notes. The source uses selected file size as a temporary stand-in for part weight, or a default weight for a linked model. It then combines a setup cost, an estimated material cost, an infill multiplier, and an estimated print-time charge.

That is useful as an expectation-setting estimate, but it is not a slicer result. File size does not reliably describe the geometry, wall count, support requirement, material volume, or print time. The interface should label this distinction clearly so a customer understands that the final quote follows model review.

### Make visual preference persistent without making it account data
The theme switcher stores light/dark mode and the selected visual style in local storage. This makes the experience feel consistent for a returning visitor without requiring authentication or sending a preference to a server.

The project includes Firebase dependencies and an admin route, but the reviewed custom-order flow currently simulates a successful submission in the browser. The source reviewed here does not show a file upload or an order record being written to a backend.

## Result
Faza3D demonstrates a useful separation between standard products and custom fabrication. The gallery supports both parts of the story: a public-facing shop interface and real printing equipment and outputs.

The custom-order estimate is a frontend planning aid, not a confirmed quote, and the submitted request is not yet persisted by the reviewed code. Those boundaries matter because manufacturing promises should come from geometry and machine planning, not from a polished form alone.

## What I would improve
I would move models to private object storage, run a server-side parser for supported formats, and derive the quote from slicer output: filament volume, chosen material, layer height, support material, machine profile, and estimated duration. Each request should receive a status trail from intake through review, quote approval, printing, quality check, and delivery.

For the catalogue, the next step is inventory and order data with a proper payment or confirmed-order state. The existing Messenger handoff can remain useful for questions, but it should not be the only record of a job once the service handles more than a small number of orders.

data.title: MoviNight
data.summary: A Rust and Tauri movie explorer with filtered discovery and locally saved watchlists.

projects.body:
## Problem
Finding something to watch involves two different tasks: exploring a catalogue and remembering what caught your attention. A discovery app becomes more useful when browsing, trailers, a watchlist, and viewing history share one interface.

MoviNight puts those tasks in a desktop application. Catalogue data comes from TMDB, while the user's watchlist and watched history remain in local files. That distinction matters: local persistence removes the need for an account-based list service, but discovery and embedded trailers still depend on network services.

## What I built
The application uses a vanilla JavaScript interface inside Tauri v2, with Rust commands handling API calls and persistence. It supports movie and television discovery, title search, genre and language filters, streaming-provider selection, detail views, and YouTube trailers.

### See the application in motion

<video src="/images/projects/movinight-demo.mp4" poster="/images/projects/movinight-demo-poster.webp" aria-label="Animated MoviNight application demonstration from the project repository" width="1332" height="720" controls loop muted playsInline preload="none" style={{ width: "100%", height: "auto" }} />

The source review follows the shipped frontend in `dist/main.js` and the backend in `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`. These files show the actual command boundary and data model more precisely than the README's feature list.

## How it works
### Keep the webview-to-Rust boundary explicit
The frontend calls named Tauri commands through `invoke`. Rust deserializes TMDB responses into separate movie and TV structures, including optional poster paths and different title and release-date fields. A generic response wrapper carries results and pagination metadata.

An empty query selects a discovery endpoint; a nonempty query selects a title-search endpoint. This is a useful separation because discovery and search answer different questions. Discovery asks which items match a set of catalogue constraints; search asks which names match text. The implementation appends filter parameters, but each endpoint's supported parameters still determine their effect.

Streaming-provider requests currently use the US region. The source therefore supports provider filtering, but it does not establish availability in every user's country.

### Use a compound identity for mixed catalogues
Watched and watchlist records carry both a numeric ID and a content type. Before inserting a record, Rust removes an existing record with the same pair. That prevents a movie and a TV show with the same numeric ID from being treated as one item.

The same identity rule belongs everywhere: card state, membership checks, deletion, and persistence. If one path compares only the numeric ID, an apparently minor shortcut can corrupt the user's intent across two catalogues.

### Combine in-memory state with durable snapshots
Rust holds the API key and both lists in mutex-protected application state. The configuration directory contains separate JSON files for configuration, watched items, and the watchlist. List mutations update memory and serialize a snapshot; retrieval can load persisted records back into state.

JSON makes the storage easy to inspect and back up. The tradeoff is that each mutation rewrites a list, and a direct file write is not an atomic commit. The API key is also persisted in configuration rather than an operating-system credential vault; local storage alone should not be described as encryption.

### Design the surrounding states
The frontend distinguishes loading, empty, error, and result views. Pagination appends new cards rather than replacing the whole list, while missing poster paths use a fallback immediately. Trailer selection happens in Rust, keeping another piece of API interpretation outside the rendering code.

## Result
The [MoviNight repository](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight) contains a complete discovery-to-tracking workflow built around a small command interface. Its most reusable idea is pairing a web UI with native persistence while keeping media identity consistent across lists.

This case study is based on source inspection, rather than a new installer or performance benchmark. Platform support and speed need separate runtime verification; the README's operating-system claims are not treated as measured compatibility here.

## What I would improve
I would reuse a configured HTTP client with timeouts and explicit status handling, make provider region selectable, and add cancellation or request-version guards so an older search cannot overwrite newer results. Persistence should write a temporary file and replace the destination atomically, while API keys should use platform credential storage.

The most useful tests would exercise movie/TV ID collisions, malformed saved JSON, interrupted writes, and pagination after a filter change. These target the boundaries that can damage a watchlist, rather than merely checking that a card renders.

Source references: [Rust commands and persistence](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight/blob/main/src-tauri/src/lib.rs), [shipped JavaScript frontend](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight/blob/main/dist/main.js).

data.title: NiotoShield
data.summary: CUDA-ready vehicle vision security: anti-spoofing, embeddings, and controlled access.

projects.body:
## Problem

NiotoShield asks a difficult edge-AI question: how can a vehicle-security device decide quickly enough to be useful, without treating every detected face as trustworthy? Face recognition alone is not sufficient. A printed portrait or replayed screen can pass a recognizer unless liveness is checked first.

The system therefore needs two distinct gates: an anti-spoofing decision before identity matching, then a local authorization decision after a match. It also needs a safe way to refresh the enrolled identities without shipping a new firmware image every time a profile changes.

## What I built

I built NiotoShield as a graduation project that joins a camera, Raspberry Pi software, custom electronics, cloud-backed enrollment, and a vehicle-access output. The device is provisioned with a product key, synchronizes its owner profile from Supabase, converts the approved images into local face embeddings, and keeps the recognition path local at scan time.

The public [NiotoShield firmware repository](https://github.com/mahostar/NiotoShield-Firmware) documents the provisioning and recognition side: environment-based credentials, product-key lookup, image download, update tracking, embedding generation, and local matching. It deliberately avoids keeping the downloaded enrollment photos after embeddings are generated.

The liveness side became [EasyShield](/projects/easyshield), a separate open-source anti-spoofing project. That separation matters: NiotoShield owns the access-control flow, while EasyShield owns the data preparation, model training, evaluation, and live Real/Fake inference workflow.

## How it works

### A two-gate vision path

The sequence diagram in the project gallery shows the intended runtime path. The camera captures a short set of face images. EasyShield evaluates the frames for spoofing before the recognizer is allowed to compare identity embeddings. A spoofing result ends the flow immediately; a verified face is compared with the locally stored enrollment vectors. A match above the decision threshold authorizes the output that activates vehicle access.

The design is intentionally ordered this way. Running identity matching on an unverified face would make the recognizer the first security boundary, which is the wrong place to detect a printed or replayed attack. Anti-spoofing reduces that risk before the access relay is involved.

### Enrollment and synchronization

The firmware uses the device product key to retrieve the associated user profile. It compares the profile's `updated_at` value with its last successful synchronization, so it only rebuilds the local image and embedding data when the enrollment changes. This keeps the recognition path independent from round-trip cloud latency while allowing a profile to be updated remotely.

InsightFace generates the face embeddings, which are stored with metadata for later comparison. The public firmware README documents a default similarity threshold of `0.5`. The supplied system diagram shows a 70% decision point, so a deployment should make the final operating threshold explicit and validate it against false-accept and false-reject rates instead of leaving two different representations of the rule.

### CUDA is part of the deployment contract

The acceleration story is about the whole inference stack, not a CUDA label on a project. EasyShield documents a CUDA 11.8 and cuDNN 8.9.6 setup with a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build (`cu118`) for its YOLOv12-nano anti-spoofing model. Its published 8,000-image evaluation reports a 75.47 ms average inference time, while the hardware sequence diagram frames a sub-80 ms analysis target. Those figures describe the model evaluation and design target; they are not a guarantee of end-to-end latency on every device or camera.

For an NVIDIA edge target such as Jetson, the deployment path is JetPack, CUDA, cuDNN, and TensorRT. CUDA accelerates the neural-network work; camera capture, decoding, data movement, thresholding, cloud synchronization, and relay actuation still have their own cost. Treating these as separate stages is how I reason about whether a vision pipeline can feel real-time rather than only reporting a fast model benchmark.

The current public repositories document the CUDA/cuDNN PyTorch environment and the Edge/Jetson runtime prerequisites. They do not include a committed TensorRT engine or an INT8 calibration pipeline, so those belong in the next deployment phase rather than being claimed as already shipped.

## Result

NiotoShield demonstrates a complete security chain: provisioned profile sync, local embedding generation, anti-spoofing before matching, a thresholded identity decision, and a physical authorization step. The result is a more credible edge-security architecture than a standalone face-recognition demo because the model, identity store, update mechanism, and output action all have a defined place.

EasyShield supports the model side with its own [open-source repository](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5): YOLOv12-nano training tools, MTCNN-assisted face preparation, live testing, and CUDA-aware environment guidance. Together, the two repositories show the link between model work and a hardware system that can use it.

## What I would improve

The next technical milestone is a measured edge deployment. I would profile camera-to-decision latency stage by stage on the target hardware, publish the camera resolution and batch policy, and separate anti-spoofing latency from face-embedding and similarity latency. On Jetson, I would export and validate a TensorRT engine, test FP16 first, then evaluate INT8 only with a representative calibration set and accuracy checks.

I would also unify the matching threshold across the design diagram and firmware, test replay attacks and poor lighting, rotate product credentials, make synchronization recover safely after interruption, and document the relay's fail-safe behavior. Those details turn a promising vision pipeline into an auditable access-control system.

data.title: Plantini
data.summary: Hydroponic towers connecting custom sensing, ESP32 firmware, and in-house fabrication.

projects.body:
## Problem

In hydroponics, the nutrient reservoir is part of the product. A plant can only receive a consistent recipe if the controller has a credible picture of what is in the water. Plantini needed a sensor path that could turn a changing nutrient solution into a usable signal for its ESP32 controller and dosing decisions.

Commercial AC TDS options were expensive and difficult to source for the product we were building. That made the sensor a core engineering problem rather than an off-the-shelf purchase: Plantini needed a design it could understand, control, and produce as part of its own hardware.

The challenge is not merely reading a number. A reading must be repeatable enough to support a target, stable enough to distinguish a real nutrient change from measurement noise, and maintainable enough to work in a real growing system rather than only on a bench.

## What I built

As a co-founder, I worked on Plantini's proprietary AC-based TDS sensing work and the ESP32 side that receives and acts on sensor data. **We created proprietary sensing technology and our own TDS sensor, designed so Plantini can fully manufacture it in-house.**

Getting there took four months of research and reverse-engineering competitor products. I studied the choices behind commercially available AC TDS solutions, then used that work to define a sensor path that fit Plantini's cost, availability, and manufacturing needs. The sensor design, its excitation method, analog conditioning, calibration routine, and production firmware remain private. This case study focuses on the engineering questions the sensing system had to answer without exposing that implementation.

The public project gallery shows the physical context around that work: the controller board concept, the hydroponic architecture, the tower, and the pump configuration. The sensing work connected those physical parts to a control target rather than treating the electronics as an isolated board.

## How it works

### From nutrient solution to a control signal

The sensor measures a property of the circulating solution that Plantini uses as a TDS proxy. An AC approach is appropriate for conductivity-related sensing because it avoids a persistent DC bias at the interface with the solution. The ESP32 then turns the conditioned sensor output into a value that can be compared against a dosing target.

That value is only useful when it is treated as a measurement, not a fact. The firmware has to decide when a reading is fresh, whether it has settled after a pump or dosing event, and whether a deviation is significant enough to act on. This is where embedded control starts: the measurement closes the loop between reservoir, dosing hardware, and plant environment.

### Calibration is the product work

The public record includes calibration around a 1,000 ppm dosing target. Calibration is more than selecting a scale factor. It defines the relationship between the sensor output and the operational value that the product displays or uses to make a decision. A useful procedure needs known reference solutions, repeated readings, and a way to record the conditions under which the reference was taken.

For a hydroponic device, long-term behavior matters as much as a single calibration point. Deposits, water temperature, mixing, probe aging, cable routing, and the time between dosing and sampling can all change what the controller sees. Designing around these sources of variation is the difference between a sensor demo and a system that can be maintained.

### Sensor data belongs to the system

The ESP32 is the boundary between the sensing subsystem and the rest of the tower. It receives the measurement, applies the private calibration and decision logic, and coordinates with the rest of the system. The controller has to preserve safe operating behavior when a reading is missing, implausible, or stale; a dosing action should never depend on a single unexamined sample.

The specific private code is not published here. The system design is: sense the nutrient solution, give the reading a calibration context, decide whether it is trustworthy, then use it as part of a controlled growing environment.

## Result

Plantini brought custom sensing into the same product conversation as the hydroponic tower, controller, dosing workflow, and in-house fabrication. The sensor work gave the system a route from physical water conditions to an embedded decision, with calibration around the 1,000 ppm target as an early operating reference.

It also set a standard for how I approach embedded sensing: protect the parts that are proprietary, document the engineering boundary clearly, and make the measurement's uncertainty part of the design rather than hiding it behind a dashboard value.

## What I would improve

The next step would be a long-duration sensing and dosing study. I would log raw and calibrated values, dosing events, settling time, reference checks, and maintenance events across multiple assembled units. That data would show drift, unit-to-unit variation, and the right filtering or confirmation policy for automatic dosing.

I would also define clear sensor-health states: valid, settling, suspect, and fault. That would make the controller's behavior easier to audit and would keep a bad reading from quietly becoming a bad dosing decision.

data.title: Remote PC Power Control
data.summary: An Ethernet-connected relay and dual heartbeats for remote PC power control and visibility.

projects.body:
## Problem
Remote desktop software cannot help when the computer is powered down. Solving that requires a control path that stays available independently of the PC, plus feedback about whether the controller and operating system are reachable.

A motherboard power button is a momentary switch, rather than an explicit “turn on” command. The same press can start a powered-down machine or request shutdown from a running one, depending on its state and operating-system configuration.

## What I built
The project combines a WT32-ETH01 Ethernet-connected ESP32 board, a relay across the motherboard's power-button contacts, Firebase Realtime Database, and a Node.js heartbeat process on the PC. A Flutter control application is described in the architecture; the reviewed folder contains firmware, the PC service, and design documents.

The controller has its own power supply and network connection, so it can receive a request while the PC's operating system is unavailable. This private project exposes no repository link or credentials through the portfolio.

## How it works
### Translate a request into a physical action
The control interface sets a cloud command flag. In the continuously connected firmware, a database stream delivers updates to the controller. The callback records a request; the main loop handles a one-second relay pulse and returns the relay to its inactive state.

Keeping pulse timing outside the callback avoids holding the physical action inside the network event handler. The design also separates the persistent stream from ordinary command-reset and heartbeat writes.

A successful pulse says the controller acted. It does not establish that the PC booted successfully or completed shutdown.

### Clear stale commands before accepting new ones
The connected firmware blocks relay activation while a command reset remains unconfirmed. On startup, it clears an old pending command before allowing ordinary operation. After a pulse, it resets the flag and retries failed writes.

This matters during reboot and network recovery. A flag left true must not be interpreted as a new click every time a connection returns. The guard is useful, but a boolean still lacks a unique request identity and expiration time.

### Observe two independent systems
The controller publishes its own heartbeat, while the PC service updates a separate timestamp every five seconds. The service uses the database's server timestamp, avoiding dependence on the PC's local clock for the stored value. It sends immediately at startup and continues periodically.

When the service stops, it leaves the last timestamp intact. The interface can interpret its age to decide whether contact is fresh. Separate heartbeats distinguish “the controller is reachable” from “the PC service is reporting.”

A stale PC heartbeat can mean shutdown, a crash, a stopped service, or a network outage. The honest state is “not reporting,” rather than a definitive claim about electrical power. This uncertainty matters when another press could affect an already-running machine.

### Explore latency against active time
The folder includes a deep-sleep firmware variant. It wakes periodically to check for a request, performs a pulse when needed, publishes periodic heartbeats, and returns to sleep. The sleep interval is ten seconds, with ordinary heartbeats every third wake cycle.

This reduces active time but adds polling delay and repeated connection setup. It also handles pending commands differently from the connected firmware. These are alternative strategies, rather than interchangeable guarantees; selecting one requires tests of response time, reconnect behavior, and command replay under failure.

## Result
The implementation provides an independent hardware action path and separate controller/PC visibility. It addresses a part of remote access that desktop software cannot supply: requesting a physical button action before an operating system is available.

The practical lesson is to separate requested intent, controller execution, and observed PC availability. They are related signals, but none safely substitutes for the others. This article describes the source and architecture rather than claiming a new hardware endurance or power-consumption test.

## What I would improve
I would replace the boolean flag with expiring requests carrying unique IDs, then record acknowledgements for receipt and execution. The interface should distinguish fresh contact, stale contact, and unknown state, with a deliberate action when the PC state is uncertain.

Recovery tests should cover a connection lost immediately after a pulse, failed acknowledgement, reboot with a pending request, and a heartbeat service that stops while the PC remains running. For the sleep variant, measuring wake-to-action latency and actual energy use would establish whether the tradeoff is worthwhile.

data.title: Shrinkify
data.summary: A Python media optimizer coordinating image engines and hardware-aware FFmpeg encoding.

projects.body:
## Problem
A single quality slider cannot express every compression decision. JPEG, PNG, WebP, and video have different encoders, different failure modes, and different relationships between quality and file size. A useful desktop tool must coordinate those differences without making the user build command lines for every file.

Shrinkify wraps that coordination in a Python and Tkinter application for Windows. The interesting work is the decision pipeline behind the interface: inspect the source, choose a format-specific strategy, run the encoder, and check whether the output actually helps.

## What I built
The main application coordinates Pillow, MozJPEG, pngquant, oxipng, FFmpeg, and ffprobe. It provides single-image and folder workflows, video batch processing, theme switching, saved configuration, and progress and diagnostic views.

External executables are resolved from an `engine` directory and checked at startup. Those binaries are distributed separately from the source. This keeps the Python repository smaller, while making dependency discovery and packaging part of the product experience.

## How it works
### Choose a strategy for each format
JPEG optimization prefers MozJPEG when available and falls back to Pillow. PNG optimization can try lossy palette quantization through pngquant, then lossless optimization through oxipng, then a Pillow fallback. WebP uses Pillow's encoder with a configured quality and method.

These paths have different semantics. Palette quantization can change pixels; lossless PNG optimization changes the representation without intentionally changing the image. Presenting both as one generic quality promise would hide the decision the user is making.

The intelligent image path inspects characteristics such as dimensions and image complexity, then chooses settings for the selected profile. After encoding, it compares output size with the original. If the result is no smaller, it copies the original instead. This size guard belongs to that optimization path; it is not a universal guarantee for every action in the application.

### Keep expensive work off the UI thread
Image and video batches run on background threads. Logs, progress updates, completion messages, and button state changes are scheduled back through Tkinter's `root.after` mechanism. That lets a long-running encoder finish without forcing the interface's event loop to do the encoding itself.

The distinction is useful: the external process performs compression, Python coordinates it, and the UI receives updates. The current subprocess calls often capture output until completion, so the diagnostic panel should not be mistaken for a continuous FFmpeg frame-progress stream.

### Probe before choosing a video command
ffprobe supplies video metadata used to select quality, frame-rate, bitrate, and audio settings. The command builder can choose NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync, AMD AMF, or software `libx264`. When a hardware attempt fails, the worker retries with CPU encoding.

The software branch uses CRF and a preset, while hardware branches use encoder-specific quality controls. Reusing one numeric setting does not make those controls perceptually equivalent. A future tuning pass needs separate calibration for each encoder.

The reviewed command builder emits H.264, adds MP4 fast-start metadata and `yuv420p`, and conditionally encodes audio as AAC. Although the README mentions H.265, this particular implementation path does not justify advertising a working H.265 selector.

## Result
The [Shrinkify repository](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify) demonstrates an orchestration approach to media optimization: established encoders do the specialist work, while Python supplies selection, fallback, batch handling, and understandable feedback.

The reusable lesson is that compression success has two dimensions: the process must complete, and the output must be worth keeping. The image size guard addresses the second dimension without claiming that lossy compression preserves identical visual quality. No compression ratio or throughput benchmark is claimed here.

## What I would improve
I would add cancellation, subprocess timeouts, and incremental FFmpeg progress parsing. Worker inputs should be captured from UI controls before launching a thread, keeping Tkinter access on its owning thread. Encoder selection and quality settings should move into separately testable modules; the current file also repeats a video-settings method, which makes maintenance harder.

A meaningful validation set would include transparent PNGs, animated images, JPEGs with metadata, portrait videos, clips without audio, and failing GPU encoders. Each check should compare readability, dimensions, retained metadata, output size, and visual differences. Smaller output alone is insufficient evidence of a successful media transformation.

Source references: [compression and worker implementation](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify/blob/main/Production-Ready-ts-darkMode.py), [engine setup](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify/blob/main/engine/README.md).

data.title: SmartHart
data.summary: A simulated vital-sign pipeline with seven-feature sequence classification and live charts.

projects.body:
## Problem
An isolated reading tells only part of a monitoring story. A sequence can reveal how several signals change together, but making that useful requires a consistent path from data generation to preprocessing, inference, and visualization.

SmartHart explores that path with simulated blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate. It is an academic prototype for studying sequence classification and monitoring interfaces. Its current data source is a configurable simulator, rather than a deployed patient-sensor network.

## What I built
The repository separates three responsibilities: generating labeled readings, training a temporal classifier, and running an interactive Tkinter dashboard. The dashboard plots signals, displays the predicted class, and compares predictions with the simulator's known labels.

The simulator includes normal conditions and timed anomaly scenarios. A scenario changes several signal distributions over its duration, rather than changing just one number to an outlier. Controls adjust generation frequency and anomaly probability, making it possible to explore transitions and inspect how the classifier reacts.

The supplied cover is a visual overview. The implementation details below come from the repository's Python files.

## How it works
### Turn five measurements into seven features
Training starts by validating CSV columns, parsing timestamps, dropping invalid timestamps, and sorting readings chronologically. Five measurements become seven features by adding the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure, and heart rate divided by systolic pressure with a small denominator guard.

These derived features encode relationships between signals. They are inputs to a classification experiment, not independent evidence that the system can diagnose a medical condition.

Preprocessing scales the features and encodes class labels. It groups readings into ten-step sequences, each labeled using its last reading. The configured training run uses nonoverlapping windows. A window crossing a scenario boundary can therefore contain mixed conditions while still having one target class.

### Classify a completed window
The network stacks bidirectional LSTM layers with 128 and 64 units, dropout, a dense hidden layer, and a softmax output. Early stopping monitors validation loss and restores the selected weights. Evaluation includes a confusion matrix, per-class classification report, and ROC curves, rather than accuracy alone.

Bidirectionality operates inside the completed ten-reading window. The dashboard does not require future readings beyond that window: it waits for enough samples, scales the buffer, reshapes it into one sequence of ten rows and seven features, and predicts the class of the latest reading.

### Ship preprocessing with the model
Training saves the model, scaler, and label order as separate artifacts. The dashboard loads those same artifacts and reconstructs the same seven features in the same order. This is an essential inference contract: a correctly loaded network can still produce unreliable output if runtime scaling or feature order differs from training.

After the first ten readings, the dashboard advances a sliding window one sample at a time. Its displayed accuracy compares predictions with the simulator's current labels and retains up to 100 recent comparisons. That percentage is a moving simulation result, rather than a fixed held-out test score or confidence estimate for one prediction.

## Result
SmartHart demonstrates a complete simulation-to-inference workflow in the [public repository](https://github.com/mahostar/SmartHart). The same data contract connects offline training and the live dashboard, while the simulator makes labels available for immediate feedback.

The documentation reports strong generated-data results, but those figures are not a new benchmark from this review. The more useful outcome is an inspectable experiment: change the simulation, observe a transition, and see which classes the model confuses. Resource-management extensions described in the documentation remain future work.

## What I would improve
The scaler is currently fitted before the chronological train/test split. I would fit preprocessing on the training partition only, then apply it unchanged to validation and test data. I would also isolate simulation runs across partitions so neighboring windows cannot make evaluation look easier than an independent run.

Next, I would test missing readings, noisy inputs, class imbalance, and windows crossing scenario boundaries. Per-class recall, false alarms, and inference latency would be more useful than a single accuracy figure. External datasets and a separate validation process would be necessary before claiming real-world health-monitoring performance.

Source references: [data generator](https://github.com/mahostar/SmartHart/blob/main/DataGenerator.py), [training and preprocessing](https://github.com/mahostar/SmartHart/blob/main/modelTraining.py), [live inference dashboard](https://github.com/mahostar/SmartHart/blob/main/RunTheModel.py).

data.title: TPMS Studio
data.summary: A desktop geometry engine that turns periodic surface equations into closed, 3D-printable meshes.

projects.body:
## Problem
Triply Periodic Minimal Surfaces are attractive for lightweight structures, filters, and lattice-like parts because a small mathematical rule can repeat through a volume. The hard part is turning that rule into a mesh that a printer or CAD workflow can use.

A surface equation alone does not specify physical wall thickness, part dimensions, how many unit cells fit in the part, mesh resolution, or whether the exported model is closed. TPMS Studio treats those as first-class engineering inputs instead of leaving them as manual fixes after export.

## What I built
TPMS Studio is a Python geometry engine with a desktop interface for generating TPMS shells and exporting meshes. It includes Gyroid, Primitive, Diamond, IWP, Neovius, and BCC templates, plus a custom-equation path. The interface runs generation in a worker thread, updates a 3D view, reports triangle count and watertight status, and exports the current result as STL.

The configuration captures reproducible geometry: physical dimensions in millimetres, unit-cell counts along each axis, an isovalue that changes the topology and open-space balance, wall thickness, and either a target file size or an explicit grid resolution.

## How it works
### Describe the structure as a scalar field
For every point in a 3D grid, the engine evaluates a periodic mathematical function. For a Gyroid, for example, the field combines sine and cosine terms along all three axes. Unit-cell count and physical dimensions determine the angular frequency, so the same formula can repeat more densely without changing the requested part size.

The isovalue shifts the field before extracting geometry. This changes the balance of material and void space, which is why it belongs in the saved configuration rather than being treated as a cosmetic slider.

### Turn a zero-thickness surface into a printable shell
An implicit TPMS surface has no thickness. The engine converts it into a shell by keeping the region where the absolute field value falls within half the requested wall thickness. In effect, the mathematical surface becomes the centre plane of a solid band.

The engine pads the field with outside values before extracting the isosurface. That forces the mesh to close at the domain boundary instead of leaving open edges where the periodic pattern reaches the box. It then uses marching cubes to convert the sampled 3D field into vertices and triangular faces, rescales the vertices into millimetres, merges coincident points, and fixes normals.

### Choose resolution before mesh extraction
Mesh resolution controls both surface fidelity and file size. Rather than generate an excessively dense mesh and simplify it afterwards, the engine estimates a grid dimension from a target triangle budget. It also applies a minimum density per unit cell so curved features are not undersampled, and a soft cap to limit memory use.

This is a useful trade-off, not a guarantee. Triangle count depends on the formula, thickness, isovalue, and dimensions, so the file-size result is an estimate. A serious production workflow should record the actual output size and allow a controlled retry if it misses the target.

### Validate the mesh before export
After generation, the engine checks whether the mesh is watertight and reports its Euler number alongside triangle count. A watertight mesh is an important prerequisite for reliable solid printing, but it is not the same thing as a successful print. Thin walls, very small features, unsupported overhangs, material behaviour, and a slicer's settings still matter.

The application exposes hooks for curvature and periodicity checks, but the reviewed generation path currently performs the topology check directly. The custom-equation feature evaluates expressions inside a restricted math namespace; it needs stronger parsing if equations are ever accepted from an untrusted source.

## Result
The generated meshes in the project gallery show several TPMS variants produced by the workflow. The source implements the path from parameterised field to shell mesh, validation result, and STL export, with a desktop interface that keeps expensive generation work off the UI thread.

No mechanical performance, porosity, flow-rate, or printed-part benchmark is claimed here. Those properties depend on the specific geometry, material, print orientation, and manufacturing process.

## What I would improve
I would add automatic wall-thickness and minimum-feature checks based on a selected printer and nozzle profile, then run a slicer estimate before presenting a part as ready to print. The export record should include every input parameter, actual triangle count, actual file size, validation result, and a hash of the STL so the same part can be reproduced later.

For custom equations, I would replace direct expression evaluation with an abstract syntax tree that permits only approved operators and functions. I would also add a regression suite of known geometries that checks closure, dimensions, periodic boundary alignment, and mesh stability across resolutions.
